title: Do LLMs Learn from Rewards in Context? : Rethinking the role of reward in In-Context RL
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: A learning loop is probed with controlled interventions on its feedback signal and its history, showing the signal is weak and surface form matters.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, rounded title pills, takeaway pill at bottom of each
description: Three rounded panels read left to right. The left panel, in gray, shows direct ICRL. A context box holds stacked trajectory (blue) and reward (yellow) pairs, τ1/r1 through τi-1/ri-1. A red arrow feeds this context to a robot icon labeled LLM πθ. The LLM exchanges a trajectory and a reward with a globe labeled Environment, and a new τi/ri pair is accumulated back into the context. The middle panel, with a green border, is Control 1: Reward Perturbation. It shows true reward, random reward and no reward variants of the pair, beside a line chart of overlapping curves labeled Comparable outcome. A pill reads Reward effect is weak. The right panel, with a gold border, is Control 2: Trajectory Perturbation. A τi branches into noise, shuffle and crossover variants, plus a trajectory from another environment. Each variant has a bar with error whiskers beside it. A pill reads Surface matters.
caption: Direct ICRL overview (left) and controlled interventions for probing its mechanism: reward (middle) and trajectory perturbations (right).
abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) is often described as inference-time RL in which an LLM improves by accumulating trajectory-reward pairs in its context, with the reward acting as a learning signal. This framing poses a central question: is ICRL genuine inference-time RL, or better understood as a form of in-context learning (ICL)? We investigate this in the context of direct ICRL, where the model directly uses trajectory-reward pairs. Through controlled experiments on three benchmarks across six models, we find that the reward is read, but its effect is small; randomizing or removing the reward leaves the improvement curve almost unchanged. Trajectories drive improvement, but not through their semantic content: shuffled or corrupted trajectories work as well as real ones. These patterns closely mirror those known in ICL, suggesting that direct ICRL is better understood as a special case of ICL than as inference-time RL. This reframing has implications for ICRL memory design: ICL factors such as input distribution and demonstrations may matter more than RL elements such as reward shaping and exploration.
